entries.c2bfd02e99890b58754555468582f88f209ec26a: <div sID="gen3419" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Deut.4" sID="Deut.4"/> <div eID="gen3419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3420" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3421" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A most earnest and pathetic exhortation to obedience, both in general, and in some particular instances, backed with a great variety of very pressing arguments, repeated again and again, and set before them in the most moving and affectionate manner imaginable, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.1-Deut.4.40">ver. 1-40</reference>. II. The appointing of the cities of refuge on that side Jordan, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.41-Deut.4.43">ver. 41-43</reference>. III. The particular description of the place where Moses delivered the following repetition of the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.44-Deut.4.49">ver. 44</reference>, &c.

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3422" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now therefore hearken, O Israel, unto the statutes and unto the judgments, which I teach you, for to do <hi type="italic">them,</hi> that ye may live, and go in and possess the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of your fathers giveth you. <hi type="super">2</hi> Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish <hi type="italic">ought</hi> from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God which I command you. <hi type="super">3</hi> Your eyes have seen what the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did because of Baal-peor: for all the men that followed Baal-peor, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath destroyed them from among you. 4 But ye that did cleave unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God <hi type="italic">are</hi> alive every one of you this day. <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold, I have taught you statutes and judgments, even as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God commanded me, that ye should do so in the land whither ye go to possess it. <hi type="super">6</hi> Keep therefore and do <hi type="italic">them;</hi> for this <hi type="italic">is</hi> your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the nations, which shall hear all these statutes, and say, Surely this great nation <hi type="italic">is</hi> a wise and understanding people. <hi type="super">7</hi> For what nation <hi type="italic">is there so</hi> great, who <hi type="italic">hath</hi> God <hi type="italic">so</hi> nigh unto them, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God <hi type="italic">is</hi> in all <hi type="italic">things that</hi> we call upon him <hi type="italic">for?</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> And what nation <hi type="italic">is there so</hi> great, that hath statutes and judgments <hi type="italic">so</hi> righteous as all this law, which I set before you this day? <hi type="super">9</hi> Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life: but teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons; <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">Specially</hi> the day that thou stoodest before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God in Horeb, when the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Gather me the people together, and I will make them hear my words, that they may learn to fear me all the days that they shall live upon the earth, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> they may teach their children. 11 And ye came near and stood under the mountain; and the mountain burned with fire unto the midst of heaven, with darkness, clouds, and thick darkness. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto you out of the midst of the fire: ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only <hi type="italic">ye heard</hi> a voice. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he declared unto you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, <hi type="italic">even</hi> ten commandments; and he wrote them upon two tables of stone. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and judgments, that ye might do them in the land whither ye go over to possess it. <hi type="super">15</hi> Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day <hi type="italic">that</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire: <hi type="super">16</hi> Lest ye corrupt <hi type="italic">yourselves,</hi> and make you a graven image, the similitude of any figure, the likeness of male or female, <hi type="super">17</hi> The likeness of any beast that <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the earth, the likeness of any winged fowl that flieth in the air, 18 The likeness of any thing that creepeth on the ground, the likeness of any fish that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the waters beneath the earth: <hi type="super">19</hi> And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath taken you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace, <hi type="italic">even</hi> out of Egypt, to be unto him a people of inheritance, as <hi type="italic">ye are</hi> this day. <hi type="super">21</hi> Furthermore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was angry with me for your sakes, and sware that I should not go over Jordan, and that I should not go in unto that good land, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee <hi type="italic">for</hi> an inheritance: <hi type="super">22</hi> But I must die in this land, I must not go over Jordan: but ye shall go over, and possess that good land. 23 Take heed unto yourselves, lest ye forget the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, which he made with you, and make you a graven image, <hi type="italic">or</hi> the likeness of any <hi type="italic">thing,</hi> which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God hath forbidden thee. <hi type="super">24</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God <hi type="italic">is</hi> a consuming fire, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a jealous God. <hi type="super">25</hi> When thou shalt beget children, and children's children, and ye shall have remained long in the land, and shall corrupt <hi type="italic">yourselves,</hi> and make a graven image, <hi type="italic">or</hi> the likeness of any <hi type="italic">thing,</hi> and shall do evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, to provoke him to anger: <hi type="super">26</hi> I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that ye shall soon utterly perish from off the land whereunto ye go over Jordan to possess it; ye shall not prolong <hi type="italic">your</hi> days upon it, but shall utterly be destroyed. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall scatter you among the nations, and ye shall be left few in number among the heathen, whither the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall lead you. <hi type="super">28</hi> And there ye shall serve gods, the work of men's hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell. <hi type="super">29</hi> But if from thence thou shalt seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, thou shalt find <hi type="italic">him,</hi> if thou seek him with all thy heart and with all thy soul. <hi type="super">30</hi> When thou art in tribulation, and all these things are come upon thee, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in the latter days, if thou turn to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, and shalt be obedient unto his voice; <hi type="super">31</hi> (For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God <hi type="italic">is</hi> a merciful God;) he will not forsake thee, neither destroy thee, nor forget the covenant of thy fathers which he sware unto them. <hi type="super">32</hi> For ask now of the days that are past, which were before thee, since the day that God created man upon the earth, and <hi type="italic">ask</hi> from the one side of heaven unto the other, whether there hath been <hi type="italic">any such thing</hi> as this great thing <hi type="italic">is,</hi> or hath been heard like it? <hi type="super">33</hi> Did <hi type="italic">ever</hi> people hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as thou hast heard, and live? <hi type="super">34</hi> Or hath God assayed to go <hi type="italic">and</hi> take him a nation from the midst of <hi type="italic">another</hi> nation, by temptations, by signs, and by wonders, and by war, and by a mighty hand, and by a stretched out arm, and by great terrors, according to all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes? <hi type="super">35</hi> Unto thee it was showed, that thou mightest know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> he <hi type="italic">is</hi> God; <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none else beside him. <hi type="super">36</hi> Out of heaven he made thee to hear his voice, that he might instruct thee: and upon earth he showed thee his great fire; and thou heardest his words out of the midst of the fire. <hi type="super">37</hi> And because he loved thy fathers, therefore he chose their seed after them, and brought thee out in his sight with his mighty power out of Egypt; <hi type="super">38</hi> To drive out nations from before thee greater and mightier than thou <hi type="italic">art,</hi> to bring thee in, to give thee their land <hi type="italic">for</hi> an inheritance, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> this day. <hi type="super">39</hi> Know therefore this day, and consider <hi type="italic">it</hi> in thine heart, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> he <hi type="italic">is</hi> God in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none else. <hi type="super">40</hi> Thou shalt keep therefore his statutes, and his commandments, which I command thee this day, that it may go well with thee, and with thy children after thee, and that thou mayest prolong <hi type="italic">thy</hi> days upon the earth, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God giveth thee, for ever. <div eID="gen3422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3423" type="x-p"/> This most lively and excellent discourse is so entire, and the particulars of it are so often repeated, that we must take it altogether in the exposition of it, and endeavour to digest it into proper heads, for we cannot divide it into paragraphs. <div eID="gen3423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3424" type="x-p"/> I. In general, it is the use and application of the foregoing history; it comes in by way of inference from it: <hi type="italic">Now therefore harken, O Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.1">v. 1</reference>. This use we should make of the review of God's providences concerning us, we should by them be quickened and engaged to duty and obedience. The histories of the years of ancient times should in like manner be improved by us. <div eID="gen3424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3425" type="x-p"/> II. The scope and drift of his discourse is to persuade them to keep close to God and to his service, and not to forsake him for any other god, nor in any instance to decline from their duty to him. Now observe what he says to them, with a great deal of divine rhetoric, both by way of exhortation and direction, and also by way of motive and argument to enforce his exhortations. <div eID="gen3425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3426" type="x-p"/> 1. See here how he charges and commands them, and shows them <hi type="italic">what is good, and what the Lord requires of them.</hi> <div eID="gen3426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3427" type="x-p"/> (1.) He demands their diligent attention to the word of God, and to the statutes and judgments that were taught them: <hi type="italic">Hearken, O Israel.</hi> He means, not only that they must now give him the hearing, but that whenever the book of the law was read to them, or read by them, they should be attentive to it. "Hearken to the statutes, as containing the great commands of God and the great concerns of your own souls, and therefore challenging your utmost attention." At Horeb God had <hi type="italic">made them hear his words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.10">v. 10</reference>), hear them with a witness; the attention which was then constrained by the circumstances of the delivery ought ever after to be engaged by the excellency of the things themselves. What God so <hi type="italic">spoke once,</hi> we should <hi type="italic">hear twice,</hi> hear often. <div eID="gen3427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3428" type="x-p"/> (2.) He charges them to preserve the divine law pure and entire among them, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">v. 2</reference>. Keep it pure, and do not add to it; keep it entire, and do not diminish from it. Not in practice, so some: "You shall not add by committing the evil which the law forbids, nor diminish by omitting the good which the law requires." Not in opinion, so others: "You shall not add your own inventions, as if the divine institutions were defective, nor introduce, much less impose, any rites of religious worship other than what God has appointed; nor shall you diminish, or set aside, any thing that is appointed, as needless or superfluous." God's work is perfect, nothing can be put to it, nor taken from it, without making it the worse. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. The Jews understand it as prohibiting the alteration of the text or letter of the law, even in the least jot or tittle; and to their great care and exactness herein we are very much indebted, under God, for the purity and integrity of the Hebrew code. We find a fence like this made about the New Testament in the close of it, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.18-Rev.22.19">Rev. xxii. 18, 19</reference>. <div eID="gen3428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3429" type="x-p"/> (3.) He charges them to keep God's <hi type="italic">commandments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">v. 2</reference>), to <hi type="italic">do them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.5">v. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.14">14</reference>), to <hi type="italic">keep and do them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">v. 6</reference>), to <hi type="italic">perform the covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.13">v. 13</reference>. Hearing must be in order to doing, knowledge in order to practice. God's commandments were the way they must keep in, the rule they must keep to; they must govern themselves by the moral precepts, perform their devotion according to the divine ritual, and administer justice according to the judicial law. He concludes his discourse (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.40">v. 40</reference>) with this repeated charge: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt keep his statutes and his commandments which I command thee.</hi> What are laws made for but to be observed and obeyed? <div eID="gen3429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3430" type="x-p"/> (4.) He charges them to be very strict and careful in their observance of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently;</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">Take you therefore good heed unto yourselves;</hi> and again (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.23">v. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">Take heed to yourselves.</hi> Those that would be religious must be very cautious, and walk circumspectly. Considering how many temptations we are compassed about with, and what corrupt inclinations we have in our own bosoms, we have great need to look about us and to keep our hearts with all diligence. Those cannot walk aright that walk carelessly and at all adventures. <div eID="gen3430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3431" type="x-p"/> (5.) He charges them particularly to take heed of the sin of idolatry, that sin which of all others they would be most tempted to by the customs of the nations, which they were most addicted to by the corruption of their hearts, and which would be most provoking to God and of the most pernicious consequences to themselves: <hi type="italic">Take good heed,</hi> lest in this matter <hi type="italic">you corrupt yourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.15-Deut.4.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. Two sorts of idolatry he cautions them against:—[1.] The worship of images, however by them they might intend to worship the true God, as they had done in the golden calf, so changing the <hi type="italic">truth of God into a lie</hi> and his <hi type="italic">glory into shame.</hi> The second commandment is expressly directed against this, and is here enlarged upon, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.15-Deut.4.18">v. 15-18</reference>. "Take heed <hi type="italic">lest you corrupt yourselves,</hi>" that is, "lest you debauch yourselves;" for those that think to make images of God form in their minds such notions of him as must needs be an inlet to all impieties; and it is intimated that it is a spiritual adultery. "And take heed lest you destroy yourselves. If any thing ruin you, this will be it. Whatever you do, make no similitude of God, either in a human shape, <hi type="italic">male of female,</hi> or in the shape of any <hi type="italic">beast or fowl, serpent or fish;</hi>" for the heathen worshipped their gods by images of all these kinds, being either not able to form, or not willing to admit, that plain demonstration which we find, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">Hos. viii. 6</reference>: <hi type="italic">The workman made it, therefore it is not God.</hi> To represent an infinite Spirit by an image, and the great Creator by the image of a creature, is the greatest affront we can put upon God and the greatest cheat we can put upon ourselves. As an argument against their making images of God, he urges it very much upon them that when God made himself known to them at Horeb he did it by a voice of words which sounded in their ears, to teach them that <hi type="italic">faith comes by hearing,</hi> and God in the word is nigh us; but no image was presented to their eye, for to see God as he is is reserved for our happiness in the other world, and to see him as he is not will do us hurt and no good in this world. You saw <hi type="italic">no similitude</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">no manner of similitude,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.15">v. 15</reference>. Probably they expected to have seen some similitude, for they were ready to <hi type="italic">break through unto the Lord to gaze,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.21">Exod. xix. 21</reference>. But all they saw was <hi type="italic">light</hi> and <hi type="italic">fire,</hi> and nothing that they could make an image of, God an infinite wisdom so ordering his manifestation of himself because of the <hi type="italic">peril of idolatry.</hi> It is said indeed of Moses that he <hi type="italic">beheld the similitude of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.12.8">Num. xii. 8</reference>), God allowing him that favour because he was above the temptation of idolatry; but for the people who had lately come from admiring the idols of Egypt, they must see no resemblance of God, lest they should have pretended to copy it, and so should have received the second commandment in vain; "for" (says bishop Patrick) "they would have thought that this forbade them only to make any representation of God besides that wherein he showed himself to them, in which they would have concluded it lawful to represent him." Let this be a caution to us to take heed of making images of God in our fancy and imagination when we are worshipping him, lest thereby we corrupt ourselves. There may be idols in the heart, where there are none in the sanctuary. [2.] The worship of the sun, moon, and stars, is another sort of idolatry which they were cautioned against, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">v. 19</reference>. This was the most ancient species of idolatry and the most plausible, drawing the adoration to those creatures that not only are in a situation above us, but are most sensibly glorious in themselves and most generally serviceable to the world. And the plausibleness of it made it the more dangerous. It is intimated here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How strong the temptation is to sense; for the caution is, <hi type="italic">Lest thou shouldest be driven to worship them</hi> by the strong impulse of a vain imagination and the impetuous torrent of the customs of the nations. The heart is supposed to <hi type="italic">walk after the eye,</hi> which, in our corrupt and degenerate state, it is very apt to do. "<hi type="italic">When thou seest the sun, moon, and stars,</hi> thou wilt so admire their height and brightness, their regular motion and powerful influence, that thou wilt be strongly tempted to give that glory to them which is due to him that made them, and made them what they are to us—gave them their beings, and made them blessings to the world." It seems there was need of a great deal of resolution to arm them against this temptation, so weak was their faith in an invisible God and an invisible world. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Yet he shows how weak the temptation would be to those that would use their reason; for these pretended deities, the <hi type="italic">sun, moon, and stars,</hi> were only blessings which the Lord their God, whom they were obliged to worship, had imparted to all nations. It is absurd to worship them, for they are man's servants, were made and ordained to give light on earth; and shall we serve those that were made to serve us? The sun, in Hebrew is called <hi type="italic">shemesh,</hi> which signifies a <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> for it is the minister-general of this visible world, and holds the candle to all mankind; let it not then be worshipped as a lord. Moreover, they are God's gifts; he has imparted them; whatever benefit we have by them, we owe it to him; it is therefore highly injurious to him to give that honour and praise to them which is due to him only. <div eID="gen3431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3432" type="x-p"/> (6.) He charges them to teach their children to observe the laws of God: <hi type="italic">Teach them to thy sons, and thy sons' sons</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">that they may teach their children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.10">v. 10</reference>. [1.] Care must be taken in general to preserve the entail of religion among them, and to transmit the knowledge and worship of God to posterity; for the kingdom of God in Israel was designed to be perpetual, if they did not forfeit the privilege of it. [2.] Parents must, in order hereunto, particularly take care to teach their own children the fear of God, and to train them up in an observance of all his commandments. <div eID="gen3432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3433" type="x-p"/> (7.) He charges them never to forget their duty: <hi type="italic">Take heed lest you forget the covenant of the Lord your God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.23">v. 23</reference>. Though God is ever mindful of the covenant, we are apt to forget it; and this is at the bottom of all our departures from God. We have need therefore to watch against all those things which would put the covenant out of our minds, and to watch over our own hearts, lest at any time we let it slip; and so we must take heed lest at any time we forget our religion, lest we lose it or leave it off. Care and caution, and holy watchfulness, are the best helps against a bad memory. These are the directions and commands he gives them. <div eID="gen3433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3434" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us see now what are the motives or arguments with which he backs these exhortations. How does he order the cause before them, and fill his mouth with arguments! He has a great deal to say on God's behalf. Some of his topics are indeed peculiar to that people, yet applicable to us. But, upon the whole, it is evident that religion has reason on its side, the powerful charms of which all that are irreligious wilfully stop their ears against. <div eID="gen3434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3435" type="x-p"/> (1.) He urges the greatness, glory, and goodness, of God. Did we consider what a God he is with whom we have to do, we should surely make conscience of our duty to him and not dare to sin against him. He reminds them here, [1.] That the Lord Jehovah is the <hi type="italic">one and only living and true God.</hi> This they must <hi type="italic">know and consider,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.39">v. 39</reference>. There are many things which we know, but are not the better for, because we do not consider them, we do not apply them to ourselves, nor draw proper inferences from them. This is a truth so evident that it cannot but be known, and so influential that, if it were duly considered, it would effectually reform the world, <hi type="italic">That the Lord Jehovah he is God,</hi> an infinite and eternal Being, self-existent and self-sufficient, and the fountain of all being, power, and motion—that he is <hi type="italic">God in heaven above,</hi> clothed with all the glory and Lord of all the hosts of the upper world, and that he is God <hi type="italic">upon earth beneath,</hi> which, though distant from the throne of his glory, is not out of the reach of his sight or power, and though despicable and mean is not below his care and cognizance. And <hi type="italic">there is none else,</hi> no true and living God but himself. All the deities of the heathen were counterfeits and usurpers; nor did any of them so much as pretend to be universal monarchs in heaven and earth, but only local deities. The Israelites, who worshipped no other than the supreme <hi type="italic">Numen—Divinity,</hi> were for ever inexcusable if they either changed their God or neglected him. [2.] That he is a <hi type="italic">consuming fire, a jealous God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.24">v. 24</reference>. Take heed of offending him, for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He has a jealous eye to discern an affront; he must have your entire affection and adoration, and will by no means endure a rival. God's jealousy over us is a good reason for our godly jealousy over ourselves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He has a heavy hand to punish an affront, especially in his worship, for therein he is in a special manner jealous. He is a <hi type="italic">consuming fire;</hi> his wrath against sinners is so; it is dreadful and destroying, it is a <hi type="italic">fiery indignation</hi> which will <hi type="italic">devour the adversaries,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">Heb. x. 27</reference>. Fire consumes that only which is fuel for it, so the wrath of God fastens upon those only who, by their own sin, have fitted themselves for destruction, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13">1 Cor. iii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Isa. xxvii. 4</reference>. Even in the New Testament we find the same argument urged upon us as a reason why we should serve <hi type="italic">God with reverence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.28-Heb.12.29">Heb. xii. 28, 29</reference>), because though he is our God, and a rejoicing light to those that serve him faithfully, yet he is a consuming fire to those that trifle with him. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That yet he is <hi type="italic">a merciful God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.31">v. 31</reference>. It comes in here as an encouragement to repentance, but might serve as an inducement to obedience, and a consideration proper to prevent their apostasy. Shall we forsake a merciful God, who will never forsake us, as it follows here, if we be faithful unto him? Whither can we go to better ourselves? Shall we forget the covenant of our God, who will not <hi type="italic">forget the covenant of our fathers?</hi> Let us be held to our duty by the bonds of love, and prevailed with by the mercies of God to cleave to him. <div eID="gen3435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3436" type="x-p"/> (2.) He urges their relation to this God, his authority over them and their obligations to him. "The commandments you are to keep and do are not mine," says Moses, "not my inventions, not my injunctions, but they are the commandments of the Lord, framed by infinite wisdom, enacted by sovereign power. He is the <hi type="italic">Lord God of your fathers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.1">v. 1</reference>), so that you are his by inheritance: your fathers were his, and you were born in his house. He is the <hi type="italic">Lord your God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">v. 2</reference>), so that you are his by your own consent. He is the <hi type="italic">Lord my God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.5">v. 5</reference>), so that I treat with you as his agent and ambassador;" and in his name Moses delivered unto them all that, and that only, which he had received from the Lord. <div eID="gen3436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3437" type="x-p"/> (3.) He urges the wisdom of being religious: <hi type="italic">For this is your wisdom in the sight of the nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">v. 6</reference>. In keeping God's commandments, [1.] They would act wisely for themselves; <hi type="italic">This is your wisdom.</hi> It is not only agreeable to right reason, but highly conducive to our true interest; this is one of the first and most ancient maxims of divine revelation. <hi type="italic">The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job xxviii. 28</reference>. [2.] They would answer the expectations of their neighbours, who, upon reading or hearing the precepts of the law that was given them, would conclude that certainly the people that were governed by this law were a wise and understanding people. Great things may justly be looked for from those who are guided by divine revelation, and unto whom are committed the oracles of God. They must needs be wiser and better than other people; and so they are if they are ruled by the rules that are given them; and if they are not, though reproach may for their sakes be cast upon the religion they profess, yet it will in the end certainly return upon themselves to their eternal confusion. Those that enjoy the benefit of divine light and laws ought to conduct themselves so as to support their own reputation for wisdom and honour (see <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Eccl. x. 1</reference>), that God may be glorified thereby. <div eID="gen3437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3438" type="x-p"/> (4.) He urges the singular advantages which they enjoyed by virtue of the happy establishment they were under, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.7-Deut.4.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Our communion with God (which is the highest honour and happiness we are capable of in this world) is kept up by the word and prayer; in both these Israel were happy above any people under heaven. [1.] Never were any people so privileged in speaking to God, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">v. 7</reference>. He was nigh unto them in all that they called upon him for, ready to answer their enquiries and resolve them by his oracle, ready to answer their requests and to grant them by a particular providence. When they had cried unto God for bread, for water, for healing, they had found him near them, to succour and relieve them, a very present help, and in the midst of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.1">Ps. xlvi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.46.5">5</reference>), his ear open to their prayers. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the character of God's Israel that on all occasions they call upon him, in every thing they make their requests known to God. They do nothing but what they consult him in, they desire nothing but what they come to him for. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that call upon God shall certainly find him within call, and ready to give an answer of peace to every prayer of faith; see <reference osisRef="Isa.58.9">Isa. lviii. 9</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt cry,</hi> as the child for a nurse, <hi type="italic">and he shall say, Here I am,</hi> what does my dear child cry for?" <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> This is a privilege which makes the Israel of God truly great and honourable. What can go further than this to magnify a people or a person? Is any name more illustrious than that of Israel, <hi type="italic">a prince with God? What nation is there so great?</hi> Other nations might boast of greater numbers, larger territories, and more ancient incorporations; but none could boast of such an interest in heaven as Israel had. They had their gods, but not so nigh to them as Israel's God was; they could not help them in a time of need, as <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.27">1 Kings xviii. 27</reference>. [2.] Never were any people so privileged in hearing from God, by the statutes and judgments which were set before them, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">v. 8</reference>. This also was the grandeur of Israel above any people. <hi type="italic">What nation is there so great, that hath statutes and judgments so righteous?</hi> Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That all these statutes and judgments of the divine law are infinitely just and righteous, above the statutes and judgments of any of the nations. The law of God is far more excellent that the law of nations. No law so consonant to natural equity and the unprejudiced dictates of right reason, so consistent with itself in all the parts of it, and so conducive to the welfare and interest of mankind, as the scripture-law is, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.128">Ps. cxix. 128</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The having of these statutes and judgments set before them is the true and transcendent greatness of any nation or people. See <reference osisRef="Ps.147.19-Ps.147.20">Ps. cxlvii. 19, 20</reference>. It is an honour to us that we have the Bible in reputation and power among us. It is an evidence of a people's being high in the favour of God, and a means of making them high among the nations. Those that magnify the law shall be magnified by it. <div eID="gen3438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3439" type="x-p"/> (5.) He urges God's glorious appearances to them at Mount Sinai, when he gave them this law. This he insists much upon. Take heed <hi type="italic">lest thou forget the day that thou stoodest before the Lord thy God in Horeb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.10">v. 10</reference>. Some of them were now alive that could remember it, though they were then under twenty years of age, and the rest of them might be said to stand there in the loins of their fathers, who received the law and entered into covenant there, not for themselves only, but for their children, to whom God had an eye particularly in giving the law, that they might teach it to their children. Two things they must remember, and, one would think, they could never forget them:—[1.] What they saw at Mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.11">v. 11</reference>. They saw a strange composition of fire and darkness, both dreadful and very awful; and they must needs be a striking foil to each other; the darkness made the fire in the midst of it look the more dreadful. Fires in the night are the most frightful, and the fire made the darkness that surrounded it look the more awful; for it must needs be a strong darkness which such a fire did not disperse. In allusion to this appearance upon Mount Sinai, God is said to show himself for his people, and against his and their enemies, in fire and darkness together, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.8-Ps.18.9">Ps. xviii. 8, 9</reference>. He tells them again (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.36">v. 36</reference>) what they saw, for he would have them never forget it: <hi type="italic">He showed thee his great fire.</hi> One flash of lightning, that fire from heaven, strikes an awe upon us; and some have observed that most creatures naturally turn their faces towards the lightning, as ready to receive the impressions of it; but how dreadful then must a constant fire from heaven be! It gave an earnest of the day of judgment, in which <hi type="italic">the Lord Jesus shall be revealed in flaming fire.</hi> As he reminds them of what they saw, so he tells them what they saw not; no manner of similitude, from which they might form either an idea of God in their fancies or an image of God in their high places. By what we see of God sufficient ground is given us to believe him to be a Being of infinite power and perfection, but no occasion given us to suspect him to have a body such as we have. [2.] What they heard at Mount Sinai (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord spoke unto you</hi> with an intelligible voice, in your own language, and you heard it." This he enlarges upon towards the close of his discourse, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.32-Deut.4.33">v. 32, 33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.36">36</reference>. <hi type="italic">First, They heard the voice of God, speaking out of heaven.</hi> God manifests himself to all the world in the works of creation, without speech or language, and yet their voice is heard (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.3">Ps. xix. 1-3</reference>); but to Israel he made himself known by speech and language, condescending to the weakness of the church's infant state. Here was the <hi type="italic">voice of one crying in the wilderness, to prepare the way of the Lord. Secondly,</hi> They heard it <hi type="italic">out of the midst of the fire,</hi> which showed that it was God himself that spoke to them, for who else could dwell with devouring fire? God spoke to Job out of the whirlwind, which was terrible; but to Israel out of the fire, which was more terrible. We have reason to be thankful that he does not thus speak to us, but by men like ourselves, <hi type="italic">whose terror shall not make us afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.6-Job.33.7">Job xxxiii. 6, 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They heard it and yet lived, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.33">v. 33</reference>. It was a wonder of mercy that the fire did not devour them, or that they did not die for fear, when Moses himself trembled. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Never any people heard the like. He bids them enquire of former days and distant places, and they would find this favour of God to Israel without precedent or parallel, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.32">v. 32</reference>. This singular honour done them called for singular obedience from them. It might justly be expected that they should do more for God than other people, since God had done so much more for them. <div eID="gen3439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3440" type="x-p"/> (6.) He urges God's gracious appearances for them, in bringing them out of Egypt, from the iron furnace, where they laboured in the fire, forming them into a people, and then taking them to be his own people, a <hi type="italic">people of inheritance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">v. 20</reference>); this he mentions again, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">v. 34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.37">37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">38</reference>. Never did God do such a thing for any people; the rise of this nation was quite different from that of all other nations. [1.] They were thus dignified and distinguished, not for any thing in them that was deserving or inviting, but because God had a kindness for their fathers: he chose them. See the reasons of free grace; we are not beloved for our own sakes, but for his sake who is the great trustee of the covenant. [2.] They were delivered out of Egypt by miracles and signs, in mercy to them and in judgment upon the Egyptians, against whom God stretched out his arm, which was signified by Moses's stretching out his hand in summoning the plagues. [3.] They were designed for a happy settlement in Canaan, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.38">v. 38</reference>. Nations must be driven out from before them, to make room for them, to show how much dearer they were to God than any other people were. Egyptians and Canaanites must both be sacrificed to Israel's honour and interest. Those that stand in Israel's light, in Israel's way, shall find it is at their peril. <div eID="gen3440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3441" type="x-p"/> (7.) He urges God's righteous appearance against them sometimes for their sins. He specifies particularly the matter of Peor, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.3-Deut.4.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. This had happened very lately: their eyes had seen but the other day the sudden destruction of those that joined themselves to Baal-peor and the preservation of those that clave to the Lord, from which they might easily infer the danger of apostasy from God and the benefit of adherence to him. He also takes notice again of God's displeasure against himself: <hi type="italic">The Lord was angry with me for your sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.21-Deut.4.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. He mentions this to try their ingenuousness, whether they would really be troubled for the great prejudice which they had occasioned to their faithful friend and leader. Others' sufferings for our sakes should grieve us more than our own. <div eID="gen3441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3442" type="x-p"/> (8.) He urges the certain advantage of obedience. This argument he begins with (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">That you may live, and go in and possess the land;</hi> and this he concludes with (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.40">v. 40</reference>): <hi type="italic">That it may go well with thee, and with thy children after thee.</hi> He reminds them that they were upon their good behaviour, that their prosperity would depend upon their piety. If they kept God's precepts, he would undoubtedly fulfil his promises. <div eID="gen3442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3443" type="x-p"/> (9.) He urges the fatal consequences of their apostasy from God, that it would undoubtedly be the ruin of their nation. This he enlarges upon, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.25-Deut.4.31">v. 25-31</reference>. Here, [1.] He foresees their revolt from God to idols, that in process of time, when they had remained long in the land and were settled upon their lees, they <hi type="italic">would corrupt themselves, and make a graven image;</hi> this was the sin that would most easily beset them, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.25">v. 25</reference>. [2.] He foretells the judgments of God upon them for this: <hi type="italic">You shall utterly be destroyed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.26">v. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">scattered among the nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.27">v. 27</reference>. And their sin should be made their punishment (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">There shall you serve gods, the work of men's hands,</hi> be compelled to serve them, whether you will or no, or, through your own sottishness and stupidity, you will find no better succours to apply yourselves in your captivity." Those that cast off the duties of religion in their prosperity cannot expect the comforts of it when they come to be in distress. Justly are they then sent to the <hi type="italic">gods whom they have served,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.14">Judg. x. 14</reference>. [3.] Yet he encourages them to hope that God would reserve mercy for them in the latter days, that he would by his judgments upon them bring them to repentance, and take them again into covenant with himself, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.29-Deut.4.31">v. 29-31</reference>. Here observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That whatever place we are in we may <hi type="italic">thence seek the Lord our God,</hi> though ever so remote from our own land or from his holy temple. There is no part of this earth that has a gulf fixed between it and heaven. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those, and those only, shall find God to their comfort, who seek him with all their heart, that is, who are entirely devoted to him, earnestly desirous of his favour and solicitous to obtain it. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Afflictions are sent to engage and quicken us to see God, and, by the grace of God working with them, many are thus reduced to their right mind, "When these things shall come upon thee, it is to be hoped that thou wilt <hi type="italic">turn to the Lord thy God,</hi> for thou seest what comes of turning from him;" see <reference osisRef="Dan.9.11-Dan.9.12">Dan. ix. 11, 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> God's faithfulness to his covenant encourages us to hope that he will not reject us, though we be driven to him by affliction. If we at length remember the covenant, we shall find that he has not forgotten it. <div eID="gen3443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3444" type="x-p"/> Now let all these arguments be laid together, and then say whether religion has not reason on its side. None cast off the government of their God but those that have first abandoned the understanding of a man.
entries.4a8905ee16f49360d4efd92953a5f1f9b10507a2: <div eID="gen3444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3445" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> Then Moses severed three cities on this side Jordan toward the sunrising; <hi type="super">42</hi> That the slayer might flee thither, which should kill his neighbour unawares, and hated him not in times past; and that fleeing unto one of these cities he might live: <hi type="super">43</hi> <hi type="italic">Namely,</hi> Bezer in the wilderness, in the plain country, of the Reubenites; and Ramoth in Gilead, of the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan, of the Manassites. <hi type="super">44</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law which Moses set before the children of Israel: 45 These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the testimonies, and the statutes, and the judgments, which Moses spake unto the children of Israel, after they came forth out of Egypt, <hi type="super">46</hi> On this side Jordan, in the valley over against Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon king of the Amorites, who dwelt at Heshbon, whom Moses and the children of Israel smote, after they were come forth out of Egypt: <hi type="super">47</hi> And they possessed his land, and the land of Og king of Bashan, two kings of the Amorites, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> on this side Jordan toward the sunrising; <hi type="super">48</hi> From Aroer, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the bank of the river Arnon, even unto mount Sion, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Hermon, 49 And all the plain on this side Jordan eastward, even unto the sea of the plain, under the springs of Pisgah. <div eID="gen3445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3446" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The nomination of the cities of refuge on that side Jordan where Israel now lay encamped. Three cities were appointed for that purpose, one in the lot of Reuben, another in that of Gad, and another in that of the half tribe of Manasseh, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.41-Deut.4.43">v. 41-43</reference>. What Moses could do for that people while he was yet with them he did, to give example to the rulers who were settled that they might observe them the better when he was gone. 2. The introduction to another sermon that Moses preached to Israel, which we have in the following chapters. Probably it was preached the next sabbath day after, when the congregation attended to receive instruction. He had in general exhorted them to obedience in the former chapter; here he comes to repeat the law which they were to observe, for he demands a universal but not an implicit obedience. How can we do our duty if we do not know it? Here therefore he sets the law before them as the rule they were to work by, the way they were to walk in, sets it before them as the glass in which they were to see their natural face, that, looking into this perfect law of liberty, they might continue therein. <hi type="italic">These are the testimonies, the statutes, and the judgments,</hi> the moral, ceremonial, and judicial laws, which had been enacted before, when Israel had newly come out of Egypt, and were now repeated, <hi type="italic">on this side Jordan,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.44-Deut.4.46">v. 44-46</reference>. The place where Moses gave them these laws in charge is here particularly described. (1.) It was over-against Beth-peor, an idol-temple of the Moabites, which perhaps Moses sometimes looked towards, with a particular caution to them against the infection of that and other such like dangerous places. (2.) It was upon their new conquests, in the very land which they had got out of the hands of Sihon and Og, and were now actually in possession of, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.47">v. 47</reference>. Their present triumphs herein were a powerful argument for obedience.  <chapter eID="Deut.4"/> <div eID="gen3446" type="x-p"/>

entries.6fb00cc92b7784f85f37227433b6792653185342: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1680"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.4.1-Deut.4.13">De 4:1-13</reference>. An Exhortation to Obedience.</title> <div sID="gen2249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1680"/>1. hearken, O Israel, unto the statutes and unto the judgments, which I <hi type="bold">teach you--</hi>By statutes were meant all ordinances respecting religion and the rites of divine worship; and by judgments, all enactments relative to civil matters. The two embraced the whole law of God. <div eID="gen2249" type="x-p"/>
entries.707552e716de6b9defff98e3802a9e43e1f8500d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1681"/><div sID="gen2250" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1681"/><hi type="bold">2. Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you--</hi>by the introduction of any heathen superstition or forms of worship different from those which I have appointed (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.32">De 12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.15.39">Nu 15:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.15.9">Mt 15:9</reference>).<div eID="gen2250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shall ye diminish aught from it--</hi>by the neglect or omission of any of the observances, however trivial or irksome, which I have prescribed. The character and provisions of the ancient dispensation were adapted with divine wisdom to the instruction of that infant state of the church. But it was only a temporary economy; and although God here authorizes Moses to command that all its institutions should be honored with unfailing observance, this did not prevent Him from commissioning other prophets to alter or abrogate them when the end of that dispensation was attained. <div eID="gen2251" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b43feed48786eda6f6b0fc4b4e035aaae8730f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1682"/><div sID="gen2252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1682"/><hi type="bold">3-4. Your eyes have seen what the Lord did because of Baal-peor ... the Lord thy God hath destroyed them from among you--</hi>It appears that the pestilence and the sword of justice overtook only the guilty in that affair (<reference osisRef="Num.25.1-Num.25.9">Nu 25:1-9</reference>) while the rest of the people were spared. The allusion to that recent and appalling judgment was seasonably made as a powerful dissuasive against idolatry, and the fact mentioned was calculated to make a deep impression on people who knew and felt the truth of it. <div eID="gen2252" type="x-p"/>
entries.e06bff5f46f738c3bd6c03c1c8b609345576e568: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1683"/><div sID="gen2253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1683"/><hi type="bold">5-6. this is your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the nations, which shall hear all these statutes--</hi>Moses predicted that the faithful observance of the laws given them would raise their national character for intelligence and wisdom. In point of fact it did do so; for although the heathen world generally ridiculed the Hebrews for what they considered a foolish and absurd exclusiveness, some of the most eminent philosophers expressed the highest admiration of the fundamental principle in the Jewish religion--the unity of God; and their legislators borrowed some laws from the constitution of the Hebrews. <div eID="gen2253" type="x-p"/>
entries.a30f3ecce1eb2a56043f0a619625206573b238c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1684"/><div sID="gen2254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1684"/><hi type="bold">7-9. what nation is there so great--</hi>Here he represents their privileges and their duty in such significant and comprehensive terms, as were peculiarly calculated to arrest their attention and engage their interest. The former, their national advantages, are described (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">De 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">8</reference>), and they were twofold: 1. God's readiness to hear and aid them at all times; and 2. the excellence of that religion in which they were instructed, set forth in the "statutes and judgments so righteous" which the law of Moses contained. Their duty corresponding to these pre-eminent advantages as a people, was also twofold: 1. their own faithful obedience to that law; and 2. their obligation to imbue the minds of the young and rising generation with similar sentiments of reverence and respect for it. <div eID="gen2254" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef44e6d4275a9701d7e1380fd332acc31c58fddf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1685"/><div sID="gen2255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1685"/><hi type="bold">10. the day that thou stoodest before the Lord ... in Horeb--</hi>The delivery of the law from Sinai was an era never to be forgotten in the history of Israel. Some of those whom Moses was addressing had been present, though very young; while the rest were federally represented by their parents, who in their name and for their interest entered into the national covenant. <div eID="gen2255" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7b597daddbfc7fc87fb5e20a10d747ca1ae2b5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1686"/><div sID="gen2256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1686"/><hi type="bold">12. ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude--</hi>Although articulate sounds were heard emanating from the mount, no form or representation of the Divine Being who spoke was seen to indicate His nature or properties according to the notions of the heathen. <div eID="gen2256" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c955d8432c3db293e515429d25d8f69478e4233: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1687"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.4.14-Deut.4.40">De 4:14-40</reference>. A Particular Dissuasive against Idolatry.</title> <div sID="gen2257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1687"/><hi type="bold">15. Take ... good heed ... for ye saw no manner of similitude--</hi>The extreme proneness of the Israelites to idolatry, from their position in the midst of surrounding nations already abandoned to its seductions, accounts for their attention being repeatedly drawn to the fact that God did not appear on Sinai in any visible form; and an earnest caution, founded on that remarkable circumstance, is given to beware, not only of making representations of false gods, but also any fancied representation of the true God. <div eID="gen2257" type="x-p"/>
entries.532941a55b20f4d7b7a280ab2dd559d0a6bc6ea6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1688"/><div sID="gen2258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1688"/><hi type="bold">16-19. Lest ye corrupt yourselves, and make you a graven image--</hi>The things are here specified of which God prohibited any image or representation to be made for the purposes of worship; and, from the variety of details entered into, an idea may be formed of the extensive prevalence of idolatry in that age. In whatever way idolatry originated, whether from an intention to worship the true God through those things which seemed to afford the strongest evidences of His power, or whether a divine principle was supposed to reside in the things themselves, there was scarcely an element or object of nature but was deified. This was particularly the case with the Canaanites and Egyptians, against whose superstitious practices the caution, no doubt, was chiefly directed. The former worshipped Baal and Astarte, the latter Osiris and Isis, under the figure of a male and a female. It was in Egypt that animal-worship most prevailed, for the natives of that country deified among beasts the ox, the heifer, the sheep, and the goat, the dog, the cat, and the ape; among birds, the ibis, the hawk, and the crane; among reptiles, the crocodile, the frog, and the beetle; among fishes, all the fish of the Nile; some of these, as Osiris and Isis, were worshipped over all Egypt, the others only in particular provinces. In addition they embraced the Zabian superstition, the adoration of the Egyptians, in common with that of many other people, extending to the whole starry host. The very circumstantial details here given of the Canaanitish and Egyptian idolatry were owing to the past and prospective familiarity of the Israelites with it in all these forms. <div eID="gen2258" type="x-p"/>
entries.677b1e3bd2c1349b8307c36b937b827ea12bd91c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1689"/><div sID="gen2259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1689"/><hi type="bold">20. But the Lord hath taken you, and brought you forth out of the iron furnace--</hi>that is, furnace for smelting iron. A furnace of this kind is round, sometimes thirty feet deep, and requiring the highest intensity of heat. Such is the tremendous image chosen to represent the bondage and affliction of the Israelites [Rosenmuller].<div eID="gen2259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be unto him a people of inheritance--</hi>His peculiar possession from age to age; and therefore for you to abandon His worship for that of idols, especially the gross and debasing system of idolatry that prevails among the Egyptians, would be the greatest folly--the blackest ingratitude. <div eID="gen2260" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f11df03c5d4437e855c3477fc32c32d86ff77bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1690"/><div sID="gen2261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1690"/><hi type="bold">26. I call heaven and earth to witness against you--</hi>This solemn form of adjuration has been common in special circumstances among all people. It is used here figuratively, or as in other parts of Scripture where inanimate objects are called up as witnesses (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.1">De 32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Is 1:2</reference>). <div eID="gen2261" type="x-p"/>
entries.57455f5c7cbe8ce7e33c0c75b95d1114936cada4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1691"/><div sID="gen2262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1691"/><hi type="bold">28. there ye shall serve gods, the work of men's hands--</hi>The compulsory measures of their tyrannical conquerors would force them into idolatry, so that their choice would become their punishment. <div eID="gen2262" type="x-p"/>
entries.54ded54ccc24c6d46f7feb1a56a4edf20701f59d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1692"/><div sID="gen2263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1692"/><hi type="bold">30. in the latter days, if thou turn to the Lord thy God--</hi>either towards the destined close of their captivities, when they evinced a returning spirit of repentance and faith, or in the age of Messiah, which is commonly called "the latter days," and when the scattered tribes of Israel shall be converted to the Gospel of Christ. The occurrence of this auspicious event will be the most illustrious proof of the truth of the promise made in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.31">De 4:31</reference>. <div eID="gen2263" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea00fc1854381712a1f675997b99f319bfa9a457: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1693"/><div sID="gen2264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1693"/><hi type="bold">41-43. Then Moses severed three cities on this side Jordan--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>). <div eID="gen2264" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f950052d2475355ace1e2808f1a3fd4dfa0968d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1694"/><div sID="gen2265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1694"/><hi type="bold">44-49. this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel--</hi>This is a preface to the rehearsal of the law, which, with the addition of various explanatory circumstances, the following chapters contain. <div eID="gen2265" type="x-p"/>

entries.d3ceb86ca8480178feb423cd933cad51a794a816: <div eID="gen6476" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen6477" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6478" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6478" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6477" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6479" type="x-p"/> Exhortations to obedience, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.1">Deu 4:1</reference>. Nothing to be added to or taken from the testimonies of God, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.2">Deu 4:2</reference>. The people are exhorted to recollect how God had destroyed the ungodly among them, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.3">Deu 4:3</reference>; and preserved those who were faithful, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.4">Deu 4:4</reference>. The excellence of the Divine law, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.5">Deu 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.6">Deu 4:6</reference>. No nation in the world could boast of any such statutes, judgments, etc., <reference osisRef="Deu.4.7">Deu 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.8">Deu 4:8</reference>. They are exhorted to obedience by the wonderful manifestations of God in their behalf, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.9-Deu.4.13">Deu 4:9-13</reference>. Moses exhorts them to beware of idolatry, and to make no likeness of any thing in heaven or earth as an object of adoration, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.14-Deu.4.20">Deu 4:14-20</reference>. He informs them that he must die in that land as God had refused to let him go into the promised land, being angry with him on their account, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.21">Deu 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.22">Deu 4:22</reference>. Repeats his exhortation to obedience, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.23">Deu 4:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.24">Deu 4:24</reference>. Predicts the judgments of God against them, should they turn to idolatry, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.25-Deu.4.28">Deu 4:25-28</reference>. Promises of God's mercy to the penitent, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.29-Deu.4.31">Deu 4:29-31</reference>. The grand and unparalleled privileges of the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.32-Deu.4.40">Deu 4:32-40</reference>. Moses severs three cities on the east side of Jordan for cities of refuge, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.41">Deu 4:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.42">Deu 4:42</reference>. Their names, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.43">Deu 4:43</reference>. When and where Moses gave these statutes and judgments to Israel, <reference osisRef="Deu.4.44-Deu.4.49">Deu 4:44-49</reference>. <div eID="gen6479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6480" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen6480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6481" type="x-p"/> Hearken - unto the statutes - Every thing that concerned the rites and ceremonies of religion; judgments - all that concerned matters of civil right and wrong.
entries.53a5b3ae60943487b6cb308a5de89b1a2387ad01: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen6481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6482" type="x-p"/> Ye shall not add - Any book, chapter, verse or word, which I have not spoken; nor give any comment that has any tendency to corrupt, weaken, or destroy any part of this revelation. <div eID="gen6482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6483" type="x-p"/> Neither shall ye diminish - Ye shall not only not take away any larger portion of this word, but ye shall not take one jot or tittle from the Law; it is that word of God that abideth for ever.
entries.179f6c7e783779b387c42b248352204077486a03: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen6483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6484" type="x-p"/> Keep - and do them; for this is your wisdom - There was no mode of worship at this time on the face or the earth that was not wicked, obscene, puerile, foolish, or ridiculous, except that established by God himself among the Israelites. And every part of this, taken in its connection and reference, may be truly called a wise and reasonable service. <div eID="gen6484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6485" type="x-p"/> The nations - and say, Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people - Almost all the nations in the earth showed that they had formed this opinion of the Jews, by borrowing from them the principal part of their civil code. Take away what Asia and Europe, whether ancient or modern, have borrowed from the Mosaic laws, and you leave little behind that can be called excellent.
entries.313954b480373f846585e919e83c47191a6f9748: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen6485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6486" type="x-p"/> Only take heed to thyself - Be circumspect and watchful. <div eID="gen6486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6487" type="x-p"/> Keep thy soul diligently - Be mindful of thy eternal interests. Whatever becomes of the body, take care of the soul. <div eID="gen6487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6488" type="x-p"/> Lest thou forget - God does his work that they may be had in everlasting remembrance; and he that forgets them, forgets his own mercies. Besides, if a man forget the work of God on his soul, he loses that work. <div eID="gen6488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6489" type="x-p"/> Lest they depart from thy heart - It is not sufficient to lay up Divine things in the memory, they must be laid up in the heart. Thy word have I hidden in my heart, says David, that I might not sin against thee. The life of God in the soul of man can alone preserve the soul to life everlasting; and this grace must be retained all the days of our life. When Adam fell, his condition was not meliorated by the reflection that he had been once in paradise; nor does it avail Satan now that he was once an angel of light. Those who let the grace of God depart from their hearts, lose that grace; and those who lose the grace, fall from the grace; and as some have fallen and risen no more, so may others; therefore, take heed to thyself, etc. Were it impossible for men finally to fall from the grace of God, exhortations of this kind had never been given, because they would have been unnecessary, and God never does an unnecessary thing. <div eID="gen6489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6490" type="x-p"/> But teach them thy sons - If a man know the worth of his own soul, he will feel the importance of the salvation of the souls of his family. Those who neglect family religion, neglect personal religion; if more attention were paid to the former, even among those called religious people, we should soon have a better state of civil society. On family religion God lays much stress; and no head of a family can neglect it without endangering the final salvation of his own soul. See the note at the conclusion of <reference osisRef="Gen.18.32">Gen 18:32</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Gen.19.38">Gen 19:38</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Deu.6.7">Deu 6:7</reference> (note).
entries.92722066fb338f4971655d02f8670cb808c6b2ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen6490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6491" type="x-p"/> Ye saw no manner of similitude - Howsoever God chose to appear or manifest himself, he took care never to assume any describable form. He would have no image worship, because he is a Spirit, and they who worship him must worship him in Spirit and in truth. These outward things tend to draw the mind out of itself, and diffuse it on sensible, if not sensual, objects; and thus spiritual worship is prevented, and the Holy Ghost grieved. Persons acting in this way can never know much of the religion of the heart.
entries.47dfe98d3abb59f74f13a081832c445759ccc34a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen6491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6492" type="x-p"/> The likeness of male or female - Such as Baal-peor and the Roman Priapus, Ashtaroth or Astarte, and the Greek and Roman Venus; after whom most nations of the world literally went a whoring.
entries.7bdd94721007e228c6641b1c9e946499d437da9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen6492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6493" type="x-p"/> The likeness of any beast, etc. - Such as the Egyptian god Apis, who was worshipped under the form of a white bull; the ibis and hawk, among the fowls, had also Divine honors paid to them; serpents and the crocodile among reptiles; besides monkeys, dogs, cats, the scarabaeus, leeks, and onions! See this explained at large, <reference osisRef="Exo.20.4">Exo 20:4</reference> (note).
entries.ce2deeee501f94fb87ae0ed27b42c9fc686fcc60: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen6493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6494" type="x-p"/> When thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars - The worship of the heavenly bodies was the oldest species of idolatry. Those who had not the knowledge of the true God were led to consider the sun, moon, planets, and stars, as not only self-existing, but the authors of all the blessings possessed by mankind. The knowledge of a rational system of astronomy served to destroy this superstition; and very little of it remains now in the world, except among a few Christian and Mohammedan astrologers; those miserable sinners who endeavor, as much as possible, to revive the old idolatry, while vainly professing to believe in the true God! Nor is it to be doubted that God will proceed with them as he has done of old with the worshippers of the host of heaven. Sound philosophy is next in importance to sound divinity; and next to the study of the work of grace is that of the operations of God in nature; for these visible things make known his eternal power and Godhead.
entries.4b4b48a4a06558a16809ecd4781accf5c30a6321: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen6494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6495" type="x-p"/> Out of the iron furnace - From this mention of the word iron furnace there can be little doubt that the Israelites were employed in Egypt in the most laborious works of metallurgy. Digging, smelting, and forging of iron in so hot a climate must have been oppressive work indeed.
entries.0946c3ded1f0dc3f317b459f95dbe887aeb5449a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen6495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6496" type="x-p"/> The Lord was angry with me - And if with me, so as to debar me from entering into the promised land, can you think to escape if guilty of greater provocations?
entries.ac99ab719611a6f37b374602afcc773f47cb3619: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen6496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6497" type="x-p"/> Thy God is a consuming fire - They had seen him on the mount as an unconsuming fire, while appearing to Moses, and giving the law; and they had seen him as a consuming fire in the case of Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their company. They had, therefore, every good to expect from his approbation, and every evil to dread from his displeasure.
entries.b15de8381f80fc9d271d7703d2aadacb00e290df: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen6497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6498" type="x-p"/> I call heaven and earth to witness against you - A most solemn method of adjuration, in use among all nations in the world. So Virgil, Aen., lib. xii., ver. 176, etc. <div eID="gen6498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6499" type="x-p"/> Tum pius Aeneas stricto sic ense precatur: <div eID="gen6499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6500" type="x-p"/> Esto nunc Sol testis et haec mihi terra vocanti - <div eID="gen6500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6501" type="x-p"/> Fontesque fluviosque voco, quaeque aetheris alti <div eID="gen6501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6502" type="x-p"/> Relllgio, et quae caeruleo sunt numina ponto, etc. "Then the great Trojan prince unsheathed his sword, <div eID="gen6502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6503" type="x-p"/> And thus, with lifted hands, the gods adored: <div eID="gen6503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6504" type="x-p"/> Thou land for which I wage this war, and thou <div eID="gen6504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6505" type="x-p"/> Great source of day, be witness to my vow! - <div eID="gen6505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6506" type="x-p"/> Almighty king of heaven and queen of air, <div eID="gen6506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6507" type="x-p"/> Propitious now and reconciled by prayer, - <div eID="gen6507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6508" type="x-p"/> Ye springs, ye floods, ye various powers who lie <div eID="gen6508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6509" type="x-p"/> Beneath the deep, or tread the golden sky, - <div eID="gen6509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6510" type="x-p"/> Hear and Attest!" <div eID="gen6510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6511" type="x-p"/> Pitt. <div eID="gen6511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6512" type="x-p"/> God and man being called upon to bear testimony to the truth of what was spoken, that if there was any flaw or insincerity, it might be detected; and if any crime, it might not go unpunished. Such appeals to God, for such purposes, show at once both the origin and use of oaths. See the note on <reference osisRef="Deu.6.13">Deu 6:13</reference>.
entries.d854ea74e646a972e9f46e4d42821cfe858fb816: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen6512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6513" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall scatter you among the nations - This was amply verified in their different captivities and dispersions.
entries.ed0d6c46004cb8a823ebfbf41bc8853508a1d64e: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen6513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6514" type="x-p"/> There ye shall serve gods - wood and stone - This was also true of the Israelites, not only in their captivities, but also in their own land. And it may now be literally the case with the ten tribes who were carried away captive by the Assyrians, and of whose residence no man at present knows any thing with certainty. That they still exist there can be no doubt; but they are now, most probably, so completely incorporated with the idolaters among whom they dwell, as to be no longer distinguish able: yet God can gather them.
entries.c40807668fd8fde1731970ed4c63d60e617bbc05: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen6514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6515" type="x-p"/> But if from thence thou shalt seek the Lord - God is longsuffering, and of tender mercy; and waits, ever ready, to receive a backsliding soul when it returns to him. Is not this promise left on record for the encouragement and salvation of lost Israel?
entries.e5a3825e5d6c59bdddf261e1c95df2bf75b11e2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen6515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6516" type="x-p"/> When thou art in tribulation in the latter days - Are not these the times spoken of? And is there not still hope for Israel? Could we see them become zealous for their own law and religious observances - could we see them humble themselves before the God of Jacob - could we see them conduct their public worship with any tolerable decency and decorum - could we see them zealous to avoid every moral evil, inquiring the road to Zion, with their faces thitherward; then might we hope that the redemption of Israel was at hand: but alas! there is not the most distant evidence of any thing of the kind, except in a very few solitary instances. They are, perhaps, in the present day, more lost to every sacred principle of their own institutions than they have ever been since their return from the Babylonish captivity. By whom shall Jacob arise? for in this sense he is small - deeply fallen, and greatly degraded.
entries.bbf31305c9928dea38311ad25a72da8536626121: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen6516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6517" type="x-p"/> Did ever people hear the voice of God - It seems to have been a general belief that if God appeared to men, it was for the purpose of destroying them; and indeed most of the extraordinary manifestations of God were in the way of judgment; but here it was different; God did appear in a sovereign and extraordinary manner; but it was for the deliverance and support of the people. <div eID="gen6517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6518" type="x-p"/> 1. They heard his voice speaking with them in a distinct, articulate manner. <div eID="gen6518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6519" type="x-p"/> 2. They saw the fire, the symbol of his presence, the appearances of which demonstrated it to be supernatural. <div eID="gen6519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6520" type="x-p"/> 3. Notwithstanding God appeared so terrible, yet no person was destroyed, for he came, not to destroy, but to save.
entries.09cc2c2df39896dc44b0d8dd7f03cb42501b769e: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen6520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6521" type="x-p"/> From the midst of another nation - This was a most extraordinary thing, that a whole people, consisting of upwards of 600,000 effective men, besides women and children, should, without striking a blow, be brought out of the midst of a very powerful nation, to the political welfare of which their services were so essential; that they should be brought out in so open and public a manner; that the sea itself should be supernaturally divided to afford this mighty host a passage; and that, in a desert utterly unfriendly to human life, they should be sustained for forty years. These were such instances of the almighty power and goodness of God as never could be forgotten. <div eID="gen6521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6522" type="x-p"/> In this verse Moses enumerates seven different means used by the Almighty in effecting Israel's deliverance. <div eID="gen6522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6523" type="x-p"/> 1. Temptations, מסת massoth, from נשה nasah, to try or prove; the miracles which God wrought to try the faith and prove the obedience of the children of Israel. <div eID="gen6523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6524" type="x-p"/> 2. Signs, אתת othoth, from אתה athah, to come near; such signs as God gave them of his continual presence and especial providence, particularly the pillar of cloud and pillar of fire, keeping near to them night and day, and always directing their journeys, showing them when and where to pitch their tents, etc., etc. <div eID="gen6524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6525" type="x-p"/> 3. Wonders, מופתים mophethim, from יפת yaphath, to persuade; persuasive facts and events, says Parkhurst, whether strictly miraculous, and exceeding the powers of nature, as <reference osisRef="Exo.7.9">Exo 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.11.9">Exo 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.11.10">Exo 11:10</reference>; or not, as <reference osisRef="Isa.20.3">Isa 20:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.12.6">Eze 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.12.11">Eze 12:11</reference>.
